Chapter 5: The Value of Not Knowing—Why Questions Matter More Than Answers.
Picture this: as their conversation wound down, a quiet understanding started to settle between the two men. The younger one, who’d walked in so sure of himself, now felt the gentle weight of uncertainty. Meanwhile, the older man—despite his own struggles—seemed almost at peace with not having all the answers.
And in that moment, something clicked. The real lesson wasn’t about nailing down the perfect definition of piety. It was about the power of asking questions in the first place.
Most of us, if we’re honest, aren’t too comfortable with not knowing. We crave clear rules, straightforward answers, that sense of certainty. But what this conversation outside the courthouse really showed is that true wisdom actually starts when you’re willing to admit you don’t know everything. The older man’s questions weren’t meant to trip anybody up or win some argument. He asked in a way that made you think deeper, nudging you to look beyond what you thought you already understood.
It’s kind of humbling, isn’t it? But at the same time, it’s freeing. You don’t have to pretend to know something you don’t. You get to let go of that pressure and open yourself up to real learning. Even though the younger man left feeling a bit frustrated, he was given something valuable—a new way of seeing the world, a chance to recognize where his own understanding ended, and an invitation to keep exploring.
The value of not knowing? Honestly, it’s easy to overlook. We live in a world that rewards certainty and tends to look down on doubt. But the exchange outside the courthouse is a reminder that growth comes from curiosity. When you question your assumptions, challenge what’s always been done, and resist the urge to settle for easy answers, you start moving closer to the truth—even if you never quite get there.
The older man’s method is often called the Socratic way. And it’s not really about handing out answers. It’s about nurturing a spirit of inquiry—honesty instead of certainty, valuing the process more than the conclusion. It’s about recognizing that the biggest questions—what’s truly right or wrong, what the divine really means, or even what life itself is all about—don’t have simple, tidy answers. Sometimes, it’s the search that really matters most.
As the two men finally parted ways and the courthouse faded into the background, replaced by the soft buzz of the city, the younger man walked away with a new sense of humility. He realized that this journey towards understanding? It never really ends. And the older man, despite his own challenges, showed what it looks like to live with curiosity, to value questions, and to find wisdom even in the midst of uncertainty.
